findings.claim: Cyber is priced in two layers, not one: an attritional layer (frequency x severity from claims) and an accumulation/systemic layer priced by scenario, then capped, reinsured or excluded.
findings.value: The isolation architecture moves the attritional layer; the accumulation layer is governed by global correlation, which none of the three cases reduces
findings.source: Synthesis of Bohme & Kataria (WEIS 2006) + Zeller & Scherer, European Actuarial Journal 14:711-748 (2024), both fetched
findings.caveat: Framing is mine; each cited paper supports one layer, no single fetched source states the split this way

findings.claim: Canonical actuarial model of cyber correlation: two-step risk arrival with internal correlation rhoI (within one firm) and global correlation rhoG (across the insurer portfolio).
findings.value: Insurance is viable for HIGH internal / LOW global correlation. High rhoG causes imperfect risk-pooling, forcing high safety loadings that choke supply.
findings.source: Bohme & Kataria, Models and Measures for Correlation in Cyber-Insurance, WEIS 2006 - https://www.econinfosec.org/archive/weis2006/docs/16.pdf
findings.caveat: 2006 paper; rhoG/rhoI estimated from Leurre.com honeynet data; authors flag rhoI results as less robust

findings.claim: Bohme & Kataria's 2x2 classification puts insider attack and common-software failure in opposite quadrants, mapping directly onto the three cases.
findings.value: Insider attack = high rhoI / LOW rhoG (insurable). Worms/viruses (one software population, many firms) = high rhoI AND high rhoG (hard-to-insure quadrant). Hardware failure = low/low.
findings.source: Bohme & Kataria WEIS 2006, Table 1 - https://www.econinfosec.org/archive/weis2006/docs/16.pdf
findings.caveat: Their hardware caveat, 'unless defective computers belong to same faulty production batch', is precisely the Case 3 residual risk

findings.claim: Ignoring common-vulnerability dependence leaves expected loss unchanged but understates the tail, so naive frequency-severity pricing gets the mean right and the capital requirement wrong.
findings.value: E[S(T)] identical (55) either way; VaR(0.995) rises 76 (independence) -> 113 (common events modelled): tail understated ~33%, true tail ~49% higher
findings.source: Zeller & Scherer, European Actuarial Journal 14:711-748 (2024), Table 2 - https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s13385-024-00381-9.pdf
findings.caveat: Illustrative parameterisation of a stylised portfolio, not a market calibration

findings.claim: Annualised probability that a typical firm suffers a significant cyber incident - the frequency term.
findings.value: 9.3% in 2024, up from 2.5% in 2008 (nearly quadrupled). Manufacturing 11.2%, retail 10.9%. Sub-$100M firms more than doubled; $100B+ firms fell ~a third.
findings.source: Cyentia Institute, IRIS 2025, Figures 6-8 - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-2025.pdf

findings.claim: Severity distribution from actual cyber insurance claims - the largest such published dataset.
findings.value: n=69,683 US claims; of ~24,873 non-zero: median insurable loss $83,000; top 10% >$920,000; top 2.5% >$5,000,000. Mean is seven-figure, so mean/median ~12x.
findings.source: Verizon 2026 Breach Impact Study (DBIR companion) - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2026-breach-impact-study-dbir.pdf
findings.caveat: US closed claims only; zero-dollar claims excluded; insurable loss is not total economic loss

findings.claim: Severity is rising in real terms and scales steeply with insured entity size.
findings.value: Median $60K (2019) -> $110K (2024), +80% vs 23% CPI. SMB ~$38K, mid-market ~$96K, large enterprise ~$283K; large-enterprise top 2.5% >$22M (22x the SMB extreme).
findings.source: Verizon 2026 Breach Impact Study, Figures 4, 11, 12 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2026-breach-impact-study-dbir.pdf

findings.claim: Business interruption dominates the tail - relevant because a shared-compute failure mode is availability, not only confidentiality.
findings.value: BI has the highest median loss (~$90,000) and highest top-2.5% (~$5M); external liability median only ~$22,000 but top 2.5% just above $4M
findings.source: Verizon 2026 Breach Impact Study, Figure 13 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2026-breach-impact-study-dbir.pdf

findings.claim: Independent severity anchor from a broader (non-claims) loss dataset.
findings.value: Median total loss $603K; geometric mean $464K; arithmetic mean $14M; 95th pct $32M (2015-2024, 2024 USD). Typical loss up 15x since 2008; tail up 5x.
findings.source: Cyentia IRIS 2025, Figure 9 - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-2025.pdf
findings.caveat: IRIS median ($603K) is ~7x the DBIR claims median ($83K); different populations (disclosures/litigation vs paid claims). Use both as a band

findings.claim: CASE 1 boundary base rate: the same-OS/same-network boundary is the most exploited boundary in existence, by a wide margin.
findings.value: 502 of 1,656 CISA KEV entries (30%) are endpoint OS/app products (Windows, Chrome/Edge, Office, Adobe, Java, Linux kernel, macOS/iOS, Android). Microsoft alone: 382.
findings.source: Author count over CISA KEV v2026.07.29 - https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json
findings.caveat: Keyword classification by vendor/product string; KEV records confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, not incidents

findings.claim: CASE 2 boundary base rate for hypervisor guest-to-host, from the complete Xen Security Advisory series - the cleanest 15-year record with per-advisory IMPACT statements.
findings.value: 508 advisories 2011-2026. By IMPACT text: 45 unambiguous guest->host escalation/code execution, 64 including hedged wording, 118 loosest. So ~3-8 host-compromise advisories per year.
findings.source: Author classification of all 508 advisories from https://xenbits.xen.org/xsa/ (advisory-N.html) plus https://xenbits.xen.org/xsa/xsa.json
findings.caveat: Regex classification of IMPACT prose; the 45/64/118 spread is the honest uncertainty band. ~173 DoS-only advisories excluded

findings.claim: CASE 2 realised failure rate: hypervisor escapes are common in advisories but rare in observed exploitation.
findings.value: ~11 of 1,656 KEV entries (0.66%) are hypervisor products. Only ~4-6 are true guest->host escape: the CVE-2025-22224/22225/22226 ESXi zero-day chain, CVE-2020-1040, CVE-2008-3431.
findings.source: Author count over CISA KEV v2026.07.29 - https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json
findings.caveat: KEV under-counts targeted espionage use. Hyper-V VSP entries (CVE-2025-21333/21334/21335) are host-local EoP, not guest escape, and are excluded

findings.claim: CASE 2 vulnerability supply, independent measure from NVD.
findings.value: 43 CVEs match 'guest OS to execute arbitrary code on the host'; 302 CVEs mention 'hypervisor'; QEMU alone has 421 CVEs; 20 CVEs match 'container escape'
findings.source: NIST NVD API 2.0 keyword and virtualMatchString queries - https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0
findings.caveat: Keyword search over description text; undercounts advisories phrased differently

findings.claim: CASE 3 boundary base rate: silicon/CPU isolation boundaries have essentially never failed in observed real-world exploitation, despite eight years of published attacks.
findings.value: ZERO of 1,656 CISA KEV entries relate to Spectre, Meltdown, transient execution, speculative side channels, SGX, TrustZone or CPU enclaves.
findings.source: Author keyword scan over CISA KEV v2026.07.29 - https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json
findings.caveat: Absence of evidence: microarchitectural attacks are hard to attribute forensically, so KEV likely under-detects rather than proving zero occurrence

findings.claim: CASE 3 residual: vulnerability supply against silicon isolation is non-zero, and its correlation profile is the worst of the three - one design flaw is in every unit at once and is often unpatchable.
findings.value: 49 NVD CVEs match 'speculative execution'; 47 match 'Intel SGX'
findings.source: NIST NVD API 2.0 - services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=speculative+execution and keywordSearch=Intel+SGX
findings.caveat: Bohme & Kataria's low-rhoG rating for hardware excepts a 'same faulty production batch'; a manufacturer partition IS one batch

findings.claim: What CASE 3 uniquely removes: the internal-actor and misconfiguration category. Real and sizeable, but smaller than assumed and shrinking in the DBIR sample.
findings.value: Misc Errors + Privilege Misuse share of breaches: 33% (2024) -> 19% (2025) -> 11% (2026: 8% Errors + 3% Misuse). Within internal-actor breaches, error beats malice ~2:1.
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2026 Executive Summary p.1; DBIR 2025 pp.21,60 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf
findings.caveat: Incident-pattern shares, not actor shares; DBIR itself flags the 2024-2026 decline as partly a change in contributing partners

findings.claim: The human element persists in all three cases: Case 3 removes staff from the sharing switch, not from the business estate.
findings.value: Human element in 62% of breaches (2026), 60% (2025). Internal-actor breaches n=2,199 of 12,063 analysed (~18%) in DBIR 2025.
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2025 p.21 (Figures 18, 20); DBIR 2026 Exec Summary - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdf
findings.caveat: The 2,199/12,063 ratio is my arithmetic from figure sample sizes in the text; the figures are images and were not OCR'd

findings.claim: Initial access vectors - what attackers actually use, which tells you which boundary the frequency term is really about.
findings.value: 2026: vulnerability exploitation 31% (now the leader, +55% YoY), credential abuse 13%. 2025: exploitation 20%. Only 26% of KEV-listed criticals fully remediated; median 43 days.
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2026 Executive Summary pp.8-9 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf

findings.claim: THE DECISIVE CORRELATION NUMBER: multi-party 'ripple' events are 10x worse in the body and 22x worse in the tail. One software image on millions of endpoints manufactures exactly this event class.
findings.value: Median loss single-party $83,925 vs multi-party $854,139 (10.2x). 95th pct $17.5M vs $391.0M (22.3x). The multi-party tail is thicker, not merely shifted.
findings.source: Cyentia Institute, IRIS Tsunami, Figure 4 (from Ripples Across the Risk Surface, with RiskRecon) - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-Tsunami.pdf

findings.claim: Propagation mechanics of the largest correlated cyber events - the named mechanism is exactly what this business would create.
findings.value: 50 largest multi-party events: median cost $90.4M vs ~$200K for a typical single incident; median 31 secondary orgs, up to 800. Top propagation path: aggregated data and shared systems.
findings.source: Cyentia Institute, IRIS Tsunami, Key Findings and pp.8-9 - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-Tsunami.pdf
findings.caveat: Sample is the 50 largest events by design - severity-conditional, says nothing about frequency

findings.claim: Insiders and third parties are present even in the extreme correlated events, so Case 3's category elimination has value at the tail too.
findings.value: Insiders and third parties contributed to 34 of the 50 extreme multi-party events analysed
findings.source: Cyentia IRIS Tsunami, Key Findings - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-Tsunami.pdf

findings.claim: Ripple propagation is slow enough to observe but too fast for mid-term underwriting action - relevant to whether cover can be withdrawn mid-event.
findings.value: 25% of downstream firms are involved within 32 days of the initial event; the remaining 50% later
findings.source: Cyentia IRIS Tsunami, 'How long does it take ripples to propagate' - https://www.cyentia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/IRIS-Tsunami.pdf

findings.claim: Third-party dependency is now the dominant driver of breach exposure - the category into which a shared-compute platform places the business.
findings.value: Breaches with third-party involvement: 15% (2024) -> 30% (2025) -> 48% (2026), a 60% YoY rise. Only 23% of third-party cloud exposures were fully remediated.
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2025 p.15; DBIR 2026 Executive Summary p.9 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf

findings.claim: Ransomware is the modal loss driver in the attritional layer and the realistic monetisation path for anyone who does break out of a shared-compute sandbox.
findings.value: Present in 48% of breaches (2026), 44% (2025), 32% (2024). Median ransom paid $139,875, down from $150,000; 69% did not pay. 88% of SMB breaches vs 39% of large-org breaches.
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2026 Executive Summary p.9; DBIR 2025 p.10 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf

findings.claim: Insurers already observe the third-party channel in claims, not only in breach counts.
findings.value: Resilience reports 40% of claims had third-party involvement (cited by DBIR 2025 endnote 25, alongside the CDK Global event)
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2025, endnote 25 - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdf
findings.caveat: Cited within the DBIR; the underlying Resilience report was not fetched

findings.claim: No precedent found by direct fetch for cyber cover on a volunteer-computing or distributed-compute platform. Nearest analogues are MSP and software-supply-chain events, treated as accumulation not attritional risk.
findings.value: Analogues in fetched sources: CDK Global (DBIR 2025 endnote 25); software supply chain became a separate claims category only in the 2024 data, with a median above other breach types
findings.source: Verizon DBIR 2025 endnote 25; Verizon 2026 Breach Impact Study - https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2026-breach-impact-study-dbir.pdf
findings.caveat: Kaseya 2021, CrowdStrike July 2024 and Lloyd's bulletin Y5381 are the obvious further precedents but were NOT fetched

findings.claim: Lloyd's mandates state-backed cyber-attack exclusions on standalone cyber policies and sizes systemic cyber scenarios in the trillions - i.e. the accumulation layer is contracted out rather than priced.
findings.value: Market bulletin Y5381 (Aug 2022), effective 31 Mar 2023; Lloyd's systemic risk scenario ~$3.5trn global economic exposure
findings.source: lloyds.com bulletin and press-release URLs returned 404 or JS-only shells under curl; recalled from model knowledge, NOT fetched
findings.caveat: Verify before this becomes load-bearing - it is the key commercial fact for whether Case 2/3 can be insured without caps

notes:
CORRECTION TO THE INTUITION. "Rate of attack surfaces leading to incidents x cost of incidents" is the attritional layer only. There the three cases are closer than expected: realised exploitation of the Case 2 boundary is already rare (~4-6 confirmed guest-to-host escapes in 15 years of KEV) and of the Case 3 boundary is zero-observed. Separation is not mainly frequency of boundary failure - it is which loss categories are eliminated, and what happens to correlation.

PER CASE. Case 1 sits on the most-attacked boundary in existence (30% of all KEV) and gives the underwriter nothing to credit; shared work inherits full endpoint frequency (~9.3%/firm/yr) and severity ($83K median claim, >$5M at 2.5%). Case 2 moves onto a boundary with a measured advisory rate (Xen ~3-8 host-compromise advisories/yr) but very low realised exploitation; the separate NIC also blocks lateral movement, which matters because business interruption carries both the highest median (~$90K) and highest tail (~$5M) of the four loss types. Case 3 alone removes a whole actuarial category - internal actors and misconfiguration, ~11% of breaches in 2026, up to 33% in 2024 - but concentrates the residual into a single unpatchable, perfectly correlated design risk across the installed base.

DECISIVE. None of the three touches global correlation rhoG, which determines insurability. Expect a real quote to rate the attritional layer off DBIR/IRIS, then cap or exclude the accumulation layer.
